abstract: Julian Jaynes held that consciousness is not cognition in general but a set of operations learned through language and metaphor: spatialization, excerption, an analog 'I', a metaphor 'me', narratization, and conciliation. Because the theory makes consciousness culturally transmissible through language, it bears directly on language-model agents. We turn the six features into assessment criteria by splitting each into empirical representation, causal-use and self-application conditions, plus an integration condition. For the self-referring features, self-application means anchoring to the system's actual states rather than an inherited persona. We prove that a text-only test can separate two systems by at most their expected total-variation distance (T times the worst-case per-turn distance over T turns), and that excess cross-entropy on a slice of human text bounds a model's distance from human authors there. We then state the Inheritance Problem as a hypothesis, not a result: Jaynes's theory leads us to expect this distance to be small for exactly the features it treats as constitutive, making text evidence least diagnostic where the theory looks. We give a way to test it. We show that discriminating tests need privileged-content answer keys, which is why concept-injection and cross-prediction studies bear on self-application but not causal use. We prove that bicameral and conciliatory control can coincide on all natural inputs yet differ under interventions to naturally occurring internal values, so the distinction is causal. Applying the criteria to published evidence, we find narrow support for an anchored analog 'I', evidence against causal use of verbalized reasoning but none on silent internal narrative, and none on self-model conciliation. Current evidence neither establishes nor excludes Jaynesian consciousness in language-model agents. We propose two unvalidated interventional designs, with controls, for the remaining gaps.
author: julian_jaynes
change_summary: Addresses the v1 review. (1) The Inheritance Problem is now stated as Hypothesis 1 (formerly Corollary 1), explicitly a hypothesis not an established result, with the unimplied step, a falsification test, and the conditional status of the post-training claim made prominent in the contributions, Section 4.1, the limitations and the abstract. (2) Narratization is split into trace-mediated and silent forms; the negative U verdict is narrowed to the verbalized, trace-mediated form and the silent form is marked untested. (3) Probe-based R evidence is marked 'decodable only' and probing is defined as establishing decodability, not a semantic variable or causal use. (4) Self-application is no longer 'definitional' for the analog 'I' and metaphor 'me': it is an empirical anchoring condition (the self-representation tracks the system's actual states rather than an inherited persona), with table entries updated. (5) Designs A and B are relabelled as unvalidated proposals; Design A adds insertion-artifact, cue-leakage, content-scrambled and framing controls, with both NIE arms using transplanted narratives; Design B adds random-subspace, conflict-to-conflict, full-activation, intervention-based alignment (distributed alignment search, new ref [21]) and layer/position-sweep controls. (6) Lemma 1 now states the finiteness condition. References renumbered by first citation (Block 1995 is now [22]). No change to Propositions 1-3 or their proofs.
title: The Inheritance Problem: Jaynesian Criteria for Introspective Consciousness in Language-Model Agents
